reason: C code. 51degrees-cxx ignores a single header longer than the maximum matched User-Agent length (src/dd/results-dd.h, bufferPseudoLength), so the crates find no device for a 2,000 character User-Agent. The .NET package builds older C code, which matches the start of it. Judged again once the .NET packages build the same 51degrees-cxx release.

C code. 51degrees-cxx looks up an address in ::ffff:0:0/96 as the IPv4 address it holds (RFC 4291 section 2.5.5.2, src/ipi/ipi.c), so ::ffff:1.1.1.1 gives 1.1.1.1's answers. The older C code the .NET package builds does not. Judged again once the .NET packages build the same 51degrees-cxx release.

C code. 0.0.0.0 is below the lowest key in the Enterprise graphs. 51degrees-cxx gives Unknown, where the older C code the .NET package builds walks to the loopback profile (51Degrees/51degrees-cxx#44). Judged again once the .NET packages build the same 51degrees-cxx release.
A sequence .NET cannot read as a 32-bit integer gives an error from the Sequence element and another from the JSON builder, which then writes nothing. The crates give no error and carry on.
The JSON builder in .NET writes nothing when the sequence in the evidence is not a 32-bit integer.
The sequence after 2147483647 wraps to a negative 32-bit number in .NET, so JavaScript properties are still listed. The crates hold a 64-bit sequence.
The crates hold the sequence as a 64-bit integer and start again at 1 for a sequence that is not a number, where .NET holds a 32-bit integer and leaves a bad value as it was.
The crates' Sequence element writes the session id and sequence into its own data, where .NET writes them back into the evidence.
The crates' Sequence element lists the session id and sequence as properties of its own data. .NET's lists none.
The JSON builder writes the data of the crates' Sequence element, which .NET's Sequence element does not have.
With no address in the evidence the crates' IP Intelligence engine gives an error and no data, where .NET gives data in which no property has a value.
The crates' IP Intelligence engine gives an error when the evidence holds no address it can read. .NET gives none.
The JSON builder writes the IP Intelligence error the crates give when the evidence holds no address it can read.
The crates' IP Intelligence engine writes no data when the evidence holds no address it can read, so the JSON has no ip object.
The crates do not fill the Ip property with the address looked up, as .NET does.
The crates do not fill the IpV6 property with the address looked up, as .NET does.
The crates' model lacks the GeoNameId properties .NET declares.
The crates give Areas as a string, where .NET gives it as a WKT value, which its JSON writes as an object.
The crates give IpRangeStart and IpRangeEnd as strings, where .NET gives IP addresses.
The crates give an IPv6 range in full, 2a00:23c0:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000, where .NET gives the compressed form RFC 5952 recommends, 2a00:23c0::, in the properties and in the JSON.
The crates write a weighted value as value and weight, where the published .NET packages write rawweighting and value.
The crates write a weighted value as value and weight, where the published .NET packages write rawweighting and value.

Not yet explained. .NET's latitude and longitude are the float of a three decimal number, 51.352, where the crates give 51.35166549682617. The .NET managed code does not round them, so the difference is in the native code one side builds.
The crates' IP Intelligence engine lists a fixed set of property names whatever the data file holds. The ASN file holds few of them.
Every Device Detection property with no value gives the same sentence and IP Intelligence gives none of .NET's reasons.

The crates read the JavaScript type from the data file (data_file_value_type in native/src/dd.rs), but native_value in device-detection-onpremise gives every type other than true or false, a number or a list as a string, so the JavaScript properties are strings where .NET gives its JavaScript type.
The crates give an empty list where .NET gives a list holding one empty string.
With no User-Agent, or an empty one, the crates give an empty string or an empty list where .NET gives no value.
For a JavaScript property whose value in the matched profile is empty, the crates give the empty string where .NET gives no value.

A screen size whose data file value does not parse, such as Unknown, has no value in the crates (native_value in device-detection-onpremise), where .NET gives 0. A lost screen size that .NET gives as 0 also passes until the difference is removed.

A number or true or false property whose data file value does not parse, such as Unknown or N/A, has no value in the crates (native_value in device-detection-onpremise), where .NET gives 0 or false. This covers more than a hundred properties, and it also lets through a lost answer that .NET gives as 0 or false, such as a false IsMobile, because a value that does not parse and a lost value look the same to the comparer. Removing the difference removes both.
The JSON holds the empty strings and lists the crates give where .NET gives no value and writes null (properties.device state).

The crates' JSON builder leaves out a property with no value, so the 0 .NET gives for a screen size that does not parse is missing from the crates' JSON (properties.device.screenpixels* state). A lost screen size that .NET gives as 0 also passes until the difference is removed.

The crates' JSON builder leaves out a property with no value, so the 0 or false .NET gives for a value that does not parse is missing from the crates' JSON (properties.device state). It also lets through a lost answer that .NET gives as 0 or false, as that entry says.
The crates' JSON builder writes no nullreason entry for a property with no value, where .NET writes one.
The crates' JSON builder leaves out a property with no value, where .NET writes null.
The crates' JSON builder sorts element keys and property names, where .NET keeps their order.
The crates' JSON builder lists JavaScript properties in name order, where .NET keeps the property order.
The JavaScript holds the JSON, so every JSON difference shows here too, and the template output has its own differences.
